subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER-PROPOSED ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY BY QUEBEC LEGISLATURE-STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER-PROPOSED ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY BY QUEBEC LEGISLATURE-STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Thursday the right hon. Leader of the Opposition raised as a question of privilege the procedure before the Quebec legislature of an address to Her Majesty by the legislature on the subject of the constitutional amendment procedure. The right hon. gentleman then affirmed, and I quote from Hansard:
-addresses to the sovereign, asking for action in the British parliament, cannot, according to constitutional authorities, be made by a province or any of the provinces.
On Thursday I said I would deal with this matter at some length today, because it required to be dealt with at some length. I would like permission to do that, Mr. Speaker, in view of the importance of the matter and the strong reaction it has caused in Quebec.
So far as the right hon. gentleman's statement is concerned, that addresses to the sovereign "cannot, according to constitutional authorities, be made by a province or any of the provinces," I would be interested to know
who are these authorities; because in the study I have been able to make of this matter over the week end I have been unable to find any support for his assertion among any of the best known Canadian constitutional authorities whom I have consulted.
The right hon. gentleman also suggested that if I, as Prime Minister, were to inform the Queen-
-that it is in order that any one province may do this,
-then I would in effect have accepted the theory-
-that there can be sovereign states within this nation.
With due respect, Mr. Speaker, this statement has no foundation in fact and is quite wrong.
In putting forward this view, in criticizing the right of the legislature of Quebec to pass an address to the Sovereign, the right hon. gentleman has already provoked a strong reaction in Quebec, and quite understandably so.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, the proposed address by the legislature of Quebec reproduces the text of "an act to provide for the amendment in Canada of the constitution of Canada", the preamble of which refers to the addresses of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada requesting enactment of the act by the parliament of the United Kingdom. The address from Quebec therefore itself recognizes that action by the parliament of the United Kingdom cannot be taken unless and until the parliament of Canada has approved and submitted an address to Her Majesty.
Second, such an address can only properly be sent to the Sovereign through the Governor General. I have been assured by the Quebec authorities that this is precisely the procedure which they intend to follow, and which has been followed in the past. The Governor General, in this as in any other matter, acts on the advise of his responsible federal ministers.
Third, since this action requested in the address by the legislature of Quebec is the same as that which may be requested in an address by the parliament of Canada, it would be appropriate to advise the crown, in

Question of Privilege
forwarding it to London, in the event that it is sent forward to the Governor General through the lieutenant governor of Quebec and through the Governor General to London, that it should be acknowledged as the expression of the view of the legislature of Quebec about a matter on which action could be taken only on the basis of a decision by the parliament of Canada on the address to be placed before it.
Finally, there is ample precedent for an address to the crown from a province on constitutional matters. For example, in 1870 the house of assembly of Nova Scotia approved an address concerning Canadian confederation and the position of the province in it. In 1879 it asked, in another address to the Queen, for an amendment to the British North America Act respecting the composition of the legislative council of Nova Scotia. In 1894 Nova Scotia passed yet another address to the Queen, praying "that Your Majesty's government may be graciously pleased to recommend to the imperial parliament" an amendment to the British North America Act providing this time for the abolition of the legislative council of Nova Scotia. In 1888 the legislative assembly of New Brunswick endorsed resolutions approved by the interprovincial conference of the previous year, with an address to the lieutenant governor to convey the resolutions to Her Majesty "humbly praying Her Majesty to graciously cause her parliament to be moved to amend" the British North America Act accordingly.
Provincial addresses dealing with other than constitutional matters have also been made from time to time. For example, in 1876 the legislative assembly of British Columbia addressed a petition to the Queen respecting an alleged breach by Canada of her railway engagements with the province. In 1880 the legislative council and house of assembly of Prince Edward Island adopted a lengthy address to the Queen respecting the claim of the province for compensation for the use of its fisheries by citizens of the United States under the treaty of Washington of 1871.
Provinces have also on a number of occasions petitioned the British government direct on constitutional matters, as an alternative to an address to the sovereign. Thus in 1888 the provinces of Quebec, Ontario, Nova Scotia and Manitoba endorsed the resolutions approved by the interprovincial conference of 1887 proposing various readjustments of the constitution, and requested that they be forwarded through the Governor General to the secretary of state for the colonies. Similarly,

in 1907 the legislative assembly of British Columbia approved a resolution protesting against the financial settlement which was the subject of the constitutional amendment of that year, and requested that it be transmitted through the Governor General to the secretary of state for the colonies.
The precedents mentioned above will more than suffice to show that the legislature of Quebec is acting with constitutional propriety in the procedure it has chosen to adopt.
There is therefore, Mr. Speaker, no question of privilege, in my view, in the matter raised by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition, nor is there any substance in his contentions. The net effect of his intervention has been merely to add, unfortunately, to the difficulties that face us in trying to resolve our current constitutional problems in a way that will strengthen, not weaken, confederation.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER-PROPOSED ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY BY QUEBEC LEGISLATURE-STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has not read the authorities very carefully, if he has read them at all.

subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER-PROPOSED ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY BY QUEBEC LEGISLATURE-STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: I have read the addresses.

subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER-PROPOSED ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY BY QUEBEC LEGISLATURE-STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
As a matter of fact the statement he read indicated that he had not made any study of the subject but had simply been provided with a brief. I therefore intend to refer to some of the cases of which he has spoken.
I begin by pointing out that there is no case in Canadian history where a provincial legislature has proceeded in this way. I am going to read once more the motion which is before the legislature of Quebec:
Quebec parliament act-Motion-
That an humble address be presented to Her Majesty the Queen in the following words:
To the Queen's most Excellent Majesty:
Most Gracious Sovereign:
We, Your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal subjects, the legislative assembly of the province of Quebec, in parliament assembled, humbly approach Your Majesty praying that you may graciously be pleased to cause a measure to be made before the parliament of the United Kingdom, to be expressed as follows:
I point out that the resolution is one which is directed to the Sovereign, praying that the Sovereign will do those things which are set out therein. In other words the Sovereign is being asked by a resolution passed by the legislature of one province alone to make a most sweeping amendment affecting the dominion and every province therein.
I would point out that there is no case, as I said the other day, where a provincial

legislature has ever before passed a resolution dealing with matters under the jurisdiction of other provinces or the dominion in the terms expressly set out by me a few moments ago. As a matter of fact there have been addresses, as is generally known, passed by legislatures in respect of matters within the jurisdiction of the legislatures, and I will refer to them at some length.
Reference was made by the Prime Minister to the petition sent to the Queen in 1876 by British Columbia on the Pacific railway question. In 1881 there was a petition to the Queen on the same question, dealing with a matter within the territorial jurisdiction of British Columbia, to be forwarded to Amor De Cosmos, special agent of the province in London, to present to Her Majesty's government. This was actually presented to the secretary of state for the colonies.
Reference was also made to Nova Scotia, where in 1868 an address was presented asking for the repeal of the British North America Act in so far as it affected Nova Scotia. Again I emphasize that any address that was passed by any province at any time had to do particularly with those things which came within the jurisdiction of the province. In that case the lieutenant governor was to forward it to the foot of the throne.
In 1879 the legislative council had refused to consent to its own abolition, so the assembly passed an address to the Queen asking for an amendment to the British North America Act to empower the lieutenant governor of Nova Scotia-I again emphasize this-to add nine members to the legislative council. This address was to be sent to the Governor General, for him to forward to the foot of the throne; and it was followed by an address to the lieutenant governor informing him of the assembly's action.
In 1881 there was a motion to address the Queen, but a negativing amendment was passed. That was followed by an address in 1894 which arose out of a further abortive attempt to abolish the legislative council. In every case the address covered only matters within the jurisdiction of the province concerned. I may also refer to what took place in 1880 in Prince Edward Island in regard to fisheries.
It is interesting to note what happened after Mercier's interprovincial conference of 1887, which was the first conference at which the provinces met the dominion. Five provinces at that time asked for amendments to the British North America Act, but not one of them did so in the form of an address to
Question of Privilege
the crown or to the Queen. They all adopted identical sets of resolutions, being those passed by the conference itself, but then proceeded in different ways.
On May 26 and 28, 1888 Quebec made an address to the lieutenant governor to be transmitted by him to the Governor General and the secretary of state of Canada. Ontario followed the same procedure. Nova Scotia followed the procedure of adopting an address to the lieutenant governor to be transmitted through the Governor General to the secretary of state for the colonies. New Brunswick passed an address to the lieutenant governor to be conveyed to Her Majesty, humbly praying Her Majesty to graciously cause her parliament to be moved to amend the British North America Act in respect of the matters set out in the resolution. Manitoba passed an address to the lieutenant governor to communicate to the Governor General and the secretary of state the concurrence of the assembly in resolutions. In none of these cases did a provincial legislature pass an address to the Queen asking for amendments to the British North America Act applying to the whole country.
Perhaps the examples I have given will indicate the difficulty involved in reading general statements without examining the authorities to realize that there is a vast difference. The Nova Scotia addresses asking for amendments dealt with proposals affecting only Nova Scotia.
It is also of great importance when listening to the Prime Minister quoting what happened in 1878 and 1884 to note that those were times when we had a democratic government in Canada which was representative and responsible; quite a different situation from that of today.
There has not been one case in the last 70 years during which tremendous constitutional changes have taken place as the result of any kind of address from any province, which certainly would indicate that the changing constitutional development no longer recognizes the right of a province to even petition the crown by an address in respect of matters coming specifically within the jurisdiction of the province. Even if we were to assume that an address dealing with one province was proper in those times, there is nothing at all to indicate that it would be proper now, and no constitutional authority has taken that stand. This was a sheer facile way of speaking on the part of the Prime Minister. No constitutional authority takes the same stand.

Question of Privilege
I simply point out to him that nothing of the kind has happened in 70 years, yet in 1965 we have resolutions from various provinces to the effect that the basis of the formula for the repatriation of the constitution and also for amending the constitution, as agreed to at a dominion-provincial conference, is acceptable. The fact that there has been no case of this kind in 70 years would indicate how unprecedented is this action of the legislature of the province of Quebec. The address from the legislature of the province of Quebec does not say anything about parliament or any other legislature asking for anything, but simply says that the Quebec assembly humbly prays that Her Majesty may graciously be pleased to cause a measure to be made before the parliament of the United Kingdom, to be expressed as follows.
Sir, what the Prime Minister has done is simply to produce a red herring by dealing with a number of cases that have no reference to the terms of the present attempt at an address on the part of the province of Quebec. What has taken place, therefore, is in keeping with the kind of theory that this government plays hot and cold with, namely that there can be states within this nation. Naturally, finding there is criticism of that stand in that it is a complete denial of the whole basis of confederation, the Prime Minister comes along and plays that old Liberal tune; "When you do not agree with what a Liberal government does then you are causing disorder." In other words peace, order and good government in this nation consist in saying that Liberal governments have a monopoly in their desire for national unity.

I must admit that when I read that I was going to be brought before the bar for daring to speak in the House of Commons of Canada I was frightened. I had to ask the nature of the bar. It is an old shibboleth of Liberalism, Mr. Speaker, that when they are in difficulty they speak about unity. Yet in a period of two years this government has done more to chisel away unity by the attitude displayed again today by the Prime Minister than any government since 1867.
This course being taken by the legislature of Quebec is wrong constitutionally. The Prime Minister tried to defend it because he has to, but he was not able to produce one solitary case in Canadian history when a legislature had a petition addressed to the sovereign to bring about changes that would affect not only the province of Quebec but other provinces. It was irregular; it is irregular. All I have to say through you, sir, to the premier of Quebec is that while I am very frightened I shall be saying outside the house what I have said here.
We have not yet come to a point in Canada where the premier of any province, when he disagrees with views expressed in parliament, can say that punishment will come. I do not know what the punishment would be. I think it was provided under Edward I that in a case where disorder was caused the person would be dragged to Tyburn, there to be submitted to cruel and unnatural punishment. Beyond that I am not particularly affected by the outburst of the premier of Quebec, which indicates there was reason and responsibility and constitutional fact in what I brought before the house; and having done so, to be met by that old argument that when you don't agree with anything these people do you are-

Mr. Speaker, this is a question of privilege just for the purpose of keeping the record straight. Earlier when I asked the Leader of the Opposition if he recalled the occasion in 1943 when the legislature of Quebec petitioned the crown, he replied that he did, and that the federal government of that day condemned Duplessis for this action.
I was puzzled by this comment; therefore I have been checking the Parliamentary Guide. I find that Mr. Duplessis was not premier in 1943. Hon. J. A. Godbout was premier of Quebec, heading a Liberal administration, from November 9, 1939 until August 29, 1944. I am not seeking to reopen the argument, but I just thought the record should be kept straight.

maintopic: MR. CAMERON, NANAIMO-COWICHAN-THE ISLANDS-CUSTOMS CLEARANCE OF LETTER FROM UNITED ARAB REPUBLIC
MR. CAMERON, NANAIMO-COWICHAN-THE ISLANDS-CUSTOMS CLEARANCE OF LETTER FROM UNITED ARAB REPUBLIC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of privilege affecting not the rights and privileges of legislatures but the rights and privileges of that rather forgotten creature, the ordinary citizen. This affects not only every member of parliament but every Canadian citizen.
I have in my hand a letter I received this morning from the office of the President of the United Arab Republic, and it is clearly marked so. It was addressed to me at the House of Commons. To my surprise, and later to my dismay when I thought of the matter, I found also on the envelope this stamp; "National revenue of Canada-customs and excise-May 27, 1965-cleared by customs."

Question of Privilege
I would point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that this is a flat envelope which obviously could have contained no dutiable goods, and it raises some very serious questions in one's mind. The first is, is mail coming into Canada subject to censorship? If so, by what authority and, if so, by what criterion do the post office authorities turn it over to the customs and revenue department?
I am not concerned about it being addressed to a member of parliament; if I were a private citizen I would feel just as disturbed by this incident as I am now. I am going to turn this envelope over to the Minister of National Revenue with its contents, which he is welcome to read. I may further say it is a reply to a letter I wrote to President Nasser after I returned last year from my visit as a guest of the Arabian authorities, and I am at a complete loss to understand what authority the customs department has and, second, by what criterion do letters now come to be cleared by customs.
I am going to send this envelope over to the Minister of National Revenue. I hope he will consult his colleague the Postmaster General, and I hope tomorrow, between them, they will be able to come up with a reasonable explanation that will reassure Canadians that their mail is not liable to censorship, and they need not have the anxieties that citizens of a police state endure.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. J. Benson (Minister of National Revenue):
maintopic: MR. CAMERON, NANAIMO-COWICHAN-THE ISLANDS-CUSTOMS CLEARANCE OF LETTER FROM UNITED ARAB REPUBLIC
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would be most pleased to look into the matter raised by the hon. member, but I should not let it go a moment beyond now without assuring him that mail coming into Canada is not subject to censorship by my department.

maintopic: MR. CAMERON, NANAIMO-COWICHAN-THE ISLANDS-CUSTOMS CLEARANCE OF LETTER FROM UNITED ARAB REPUBLIC

maintopic: MR. CAMERON, NANAIMO-COWICHAN-THE ISLANDS-CUSTOMS CLEARANCE OF LETTER FROM UNITED ARAB REPUBLIC
speechtext:
I am informed that first class mail coming into Canada is sorted at the post office, and items which might conceivably contain commercial importations are turned over to the customs officers. If customs, on examining the outside of the item, decide no further examination is required, it is stamped and returned to the Post Office Department. If further examination is required, then the addressee is asked to come to customs where an examination is held in the addressee's presence and in the presence of a post office official. First class mail is never opened by my department except in the presence of the addressee.
In the case of items other than first class mail, such as parcels etc., these are turned over to the customs officers by the post office. Our customs officers then open them to see if the contents are in accord with the declaration. If this is the case they are marked "free" and mailed on to the address. If duty is due and payable, a card is sent to the addressee giving him a choice of picking it up and paying the duty or having it delivered through the post office and paying the duty when it is delivered to him. In the latter case I am referring to mail other than first class mail. First class mail is never opened by my department except in the presence of the addressee.

maintopic: MR. CAMERON, NANAIMO-COWICHAN-THE ISLANDS-CUSTOMS CLEARANCE OF LETTER FROM UNITED ARAB REPUBLIC

If it could, every letter which comes through the mail would be in that category. It was a perfectly flat envelope obviously containing nothing which would be of interest to the customs branch, and I am not at all satisfied with the answer which the minister has given me.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hunting and fishing rights of Indians is a most complicated matter, as most hon. members know. Several decisions of the courts and questions asked in this house within the past year have raised questions as to what steps the government should take to safeguard the hunting and fishing rights of our Indians.
Unfortunately over the years some inconsistencies have developed in the application of game and fishing laws to Indians in different parts of Canada. While the government of Canada has endeavoured to protect the rights of the Indians, seemingly it has not done so in all instances. Regulations have been introduced which on closer study indicate that some of the rights of, and assurances given to, the Indians may not have been adequately safeguarded.
The recent conviction of Michael Sikyea, an Indian living in the Northwest Territories, for killing one wild duck during a closed season contrary to regulations made under the Migratory Birds Convention Act illustrates the problem clearly. The court of appeal of the Northwest Territories referred to the regulations as a "breach of faith" and expressed dissatisfaction with the law as it stands.
The government recognises the seriousness of the problem, and I am pleased to announce that it has directed that an inter-departmental committee, composed of officials of the departments of citizenship and immigration, external affairs, fisheries, justice, northern affairs and national resources and the R.C.M. Police, to be chaired by the representative of the justice department, be established to conduct a comparative study of the promises contained in the various Indian treaties and surrenders as related to the laws respecting game and fish.
The committee have been instructed that their study should be directed as follows:
1.	Determining the nature and extent of the discrepancies and inconsistencies which are known to exist.
2.	Suggesting the legislative action required to carry out, in a manner which honour and good conscience dictate, the intention of the government previously announced by the Prime Minister, to do what can be done to see that the commitment originally entered

Game and Fish Laws into on behalf of King George III is maintained, and
3.	Assessing and reporting on the effect of such legislation in terms of fish and game management generally and the continental supply of migratory waterfowl, particularly.

maintopic: STUDY BY INTERDEPARTMENTAL COMMITTEE OF GAME AND FISH LAWS
speechtext:
I am sure it is with dismay that those members of this house who have an interest in the welfare of Indians and Indian rights in this country have heard the announcement just made by the minister. The announcement comes, we know, on the heels of a decision by Mr. Justice T. G. Norris upholding the unanimous decision of the British Columbia judges relating to a case involving an Indian in British Columbia who shot a deer out of season.
The cause of our dismay is the announcement by the minister that yet another interdepartmental committee is to be set up. The Indian people of this country, like the Eskimos, have a right to ask this government when they can expect some action.
In the speech from the throne made to the twenty sixth parliament we were assured that an Indian claims commission would be set up, a commission which would meet with the Indian people and come to some conclusion about settling the questions raised by these old treaties which are in conflict with laws passed by this parliament. The former minister of citizenship and immigration, who is now the Minister of Justice, indicated, when he was gathering that invaluable experience of his, that the Indian claims commission legislation would be passed by parliament or, at least introduced into parliament before the end of that session. Since that time a parade of ministers of citizenship and immigration has said the same thing, that the Indian claims commission legislation is on the verge of being presented but is being delayed while approval from Indian bands is awaited.
It is not enough for the government to set up an interdepartmental committee to study this matter. What the Indian people of this country want, and what they have an absolute legal right to get, is an assurance that they can trap and fish for food at any time of the year on unoccupied crown land. Until such time as the government gets on with its Indian claims commission legislation the Indians are justified in believing that this government has betrayed them, has given them nothing but words. They have been used


to this kind of treatment from the white man for more than TOO years now.
There is one further reason why members of this house should be dismayed. I would have hoped that the government had learned its lesson by this time. Going through the list setting out who is to serve on this advisory committee, I notice that no Indian people are to be included in these discussions concerning their welfare. I do not know how often we have to beat this government over the head. We had to fight over the right of the Quebec Eskimos to be represented when matters affecting their own welfare were under discussion; we had to fight for the right of our Indian people to be represented at federal-provincial conferences on Indian welfare. The minister's announcement does nothing to reassure the house or the Indian people that this government is fit to safeguard their well-being.

It should never be forgotten that those treaties were written by white men in the English language and explained to people who could not read or write English, and that what was contained in those treaties in no way represents the promises which were made at that time.
Thus, if members opposite want to deal with the treaties and concern themselves with the rights of the Indian people they should be prepared to sit down man to man and negotiate those treaties on a mutual basis. 1.	What variety of products were manufactured in 1964 in penitentiary industrial workshops and to whom were these supplied?
2.	If expanded sales outlets were available would these industrial workshops be prepared to increase the variety and volume of manufactured products?
3.	What effect would a substantially enlarged industrial program have on the inmate?

speakeroldname: Mr. D. S. Macdonald (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
1. In 1964 the penitentiary industrial workshops manufactured brooms and brushes, clothing and footwear for the penitentiary service. A wide variety of articles of metal, wood and textile materials were produced. These included furnishings for the institutions, e.g. furniture, shelving and housekeeping articles. Printing and bookbinding is done. Quarries produced crushed rock for the road systems of the penitentiaries. The penitentiary service utilizes approximately one half of the annual production of the shops. In addition to the penitentiary service, customers are federal departments and agencies, provincial and municipal governments, and non-profit organizations and associations, as authorized by penitentiary service regulations.
2. Subject to the demands of the main inmate training program, which is designed to produce good citizens, present penitentiary workshops have production capacity exceeding the annual output and the existing shops could substantially increase both the per capita output and the variety of products if

additional sales outlets are available and there are sufficient incentives to motivate inmate workers to put forth their best efforts. Moreover, there will be a natural increase in the size of the work force as penitentiary populations increase each year and new institutions are built and occupied. This calls for additional shop facilities and an increasing volume of sales orders will be required to train and employ the manpower available.
3.	It is the aim of the service to develop and prescribe for each inmate a program of correctional training which will redirect his criminal impulses and train him constructively for life as a free citizen. The industrial program is one element in this plan of training in skills and attitudes which are acceptable in life outside prison. In so far as the industrial program fits in with the ultimate training objective, and in motivating inmates to put forth maximum effort, an increase in the scope of the industrial program provides an improved opportunity to inmate workers to acquire saleable skills and work habits which will benefit them after release.

speechtext: Is a workroom in a city post office open to the public, that is, to the members of the mail conveying staff, the members of their families, and their passengers?

maintopic: ACCESS TO WORKROOM IN POST OFFICE
speechtext:
Workrooms in post offices are not open to the public. Regulations provide in this connection that persons other than postal workers on duty must not be admitted in the workroom of a post office unless accompanied by a responsible employee designated for that purpose. Such exemptions are necessary to allow the carrying out of maintenance and repair work or approved official visits. subtopic: CHILE-OFFER OF ASSISTANCE FOLLOWING EARTHQUAKE

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM

speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, March 26, consideration of the motion of Miss LaMarsh for the third reading of Bill No. C-136, to establish a comprehensive program of old age pensions and supplementary benefits in Canada payable to and in respect of contributors.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the case for increasing the old age security pension from $75 to $100 a month has been made previously, both in the joint committee and in this house, and for just a few minutes I wish to elaborate on that case.
One of the motions passed by the joint committee of the Senate and this house reads as follows-and I am quoting from page 2055 of the committee report:
The level of combined benefits available under the Canada pension plan and the Old Age Security

Act should be adequate for those people for whom such benefits will be the only source of income after retirement.
That motion was moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and seconded by myself, and it was approved by a vote of 15 to 5. It refers of course to the future, when the Canada pension plan will be in full operation. Our concern, now, is for those for whom the pension constitutes the principal or, indeed, the only source of income. We have to make sure that the income of these people is adequate. I maintain that $75 a month is clearly not adequate. It is true that many persons manage to get by on such an amount, but I suggest they do so only because they pay very low rents, perhaps in substandard accommodation, or because relatives help them. As long ago as 1956 the Montreal council of social agencies stated that an old age pensioner required at least $70.82 monthly to feed, clothe and shelter himself at current Montreal prices. Now, nine years later with the cost of living increased and an improvement in the standard of living expected by most Canadians, it is abundantly clear that $75 is not sufficient. I cannot say exactly what the figure should be. I recall that one of the groups which made representations before the committee-the Canadian council of social workers, I believe- suggested that a study should be made so as to ascertain the amount an old age pensioner needs. In the meantime I do not think we would err if we were to strike a figure of $100 a month. Indeed, I think such a figure would be a conservative one. Studies could then be carried out to determine what the proper income level should be.
We need to think particularly of those people whose only source of income is the old age security pension. I realize that the pension is a universal one and that everyone in the appropriate age category receives it. The other day the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) mentioned the fact that they would both become eligible for an old age security pension soon. That is quite true. However, persons in their income category are required to pay most of the money back in the form of taxation, so we should not be giving anyone too much.
At the final meeting of the pension plan committee the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre moved, and I seconded, the following resolution to be found on page 2057 of the committee report. It reads:
The committee also recommends that consideration be given to the amending of part IV of Bill
Canada Pension Plan
C-136 to provide for an increase in the pension paid under the Old Age Security Act to $100 a month and for the lowering of the eligible age for the full pension under the Old Age Security Act to age 65.
It is only the first part of the motion which is relevant here. Others have suggested that an increase in present old age pensions be paid out of Canada pension plan funds. In order to bring this about they propose that the building up period of the Canada pension plan be extended from ten years to 20 years. We reject that proposal. We want to keep the contributory earnings related plan entirely separate from the old age security fund.
By passing the motion which I shall put in a very few minutes we could achieve this result. The motion does not set any particular terms. Indeed it would be out of order if it were to do so. But when the committee reconsiders this question it should give serious attention to this proposal of $100 a month. Too often in the past increases in the old age security pension have been made at election time and used as vote getting gimmicks during election campaigns. This is a poor way to deal with questions directly concerning the welfare of our people. I suggest this is a good time at which to increase the pension. The Prime Minister told us the other day that there is no election in sight, and I believe him. Now is the time, then, for the government to put into effect the increase we are suggesting, namely an increase to $100 a month.
I therefore move, seconded by my hon. friend from Danforth (Mr. Scott):
That Bill C-136 be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole house for the purpose of reconsidering the basic amount of the old age security pension set out in clause 120 of the said bill.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Before you reach a decision on this motion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak on the question of whether or not it is in order.
This amendment to the motion for the third reading of this bill is essentially the same as the one which was put forward on Friday last and which was ruled out of order, the decision of the Chair being sustained by the house. The amendment reads:
That Bill C-136 be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole house for the purpose of reconsidering the basic amount of the old age security pension set out in clause 120 of the said bill.
In the first place, I think it is well established that we are not permitted to do indirectly in this house what cannot be done

Canada Pension Plan directly. While the amendment does not spell out the amount of the increase in the old age security pension which the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond advocates, he certainly made reference to it in the arguments he used in support of the amendment.
In the second place, I contend that this amendment seeks to alter the expenditure of money with respect to old age security pensions. Either it does that, or it does nothing at all. Again, I think it is a well established principle when considering the validity of motions that either they must seek to do something or they are out of order. If the amendment to this motion is to do anything positive, it is intended to ask the committee to change the amount as set out in clause 120 of Bill C-136. Either that, or it is nothing. There is no point in referring this bill back to the committee unless the committee is intended to do something with clause 120. Without going into all the citations which could be quoted preventing a private member from moving a motion or an amendment to a motion which would change the balance of ways and means, I think I should draw Your Honour's attention to one or two rulings. For example, citation 249 of Beauchesne's fourth edition says:
No cases can be found of any private member in the Canadian Commons receiving the authority of the crown, through a minister, to propose a motion involving the expenditure of public money.
I am sure no one will disagree that this is a principle well established in the practice of this house.
I should also like to direct to your notice, Mr. Speaker, a ruling which was made on July 11, 1963, when a question of the same kind was before the House of Commons. At that time the Speaker of the house drew attention to a ruling which was made by Mr. Speaker Casgrain on February 21, 1936. There were a number of things that he said, and I will quote some of them. Mr. Speaker Casgrain decided that a bill providing for the transfer of a government service from one department to another involves the custody of public moneys and cannot be introduced by a private member. I believe that applies to the question of whether or not it is appropriate for a private member to move an amendment to spend money either out of the consolidated revenue fund or out of the Canada pension plan fund.
Now, the hon. member stated he is not asking that there be an increase in the amount of money paid out of the Canada pension plan. However, I noticed that in the same


citation Mr. Speaker Casgrain had this to say, and I quote:
-the circumstances under which an expenditure is to be made are indivisible from that expenditure.
I think this is a case, Mr. Speaker, which lends support to the point I made a few minutes ago that an hon. member cannot attempt to do indirectly what he is prevented from doing directly. We have gone through this performance a number of times in this house when attempts have been made, either on third reading or at other stages, by private members to circumvent the prerogative of the crown by moving amendments that would have the effect of increasing the expenditure out of the consolidated revenue fund. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that you will take into consideration all of these representations that have been made, and that have been supported on division, to the effect that a member is not permitted to move this kind of amendment.
I can foresee what is going to happen if Your Honour accepts this kind of motion. Then we are going to be faced with the inference that those members who vote against it are, in fact, against the raising of the old age pension from $75 to $100 per month.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: And they are.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
The fact is that we have rules laid down in this house, and they are very clear. I am not going to refer to all of them. They are to the effect that a private member does not have this right or privilege.
Now, Mr. Speaker, this amendment fails in one other respect, too, and that is the fact that since there is to be an expenditure out of the consolidated revenue fund, a clear statement must accompany such motion or amendment indicating how much it is going to cost. For example, citation 246, paragraph (3) says that the guiding principle in determining the effect of an amendment upon the financial initiative of the crown is that the communication, to which the royal demand of recommendation is attached, must be treated as laying down once for all not only the amount of a charge, but also its objects, purposes, conditions and qualifications. Of course this amendment does none of these things.
It fails in one other respect also, Mr. Speaker, and that is that any motion putting a charge on the public funds of this country must be preceded by a resolution. Of course a private member has no right to move such a resolution. In this case obviously it is not

present. I would respectfully suggest, therefore, that as I said at the outset if this amendment does anything it is a motion to change the amount of the expenditure payable under the Old Age Security Act from $75 per month to $100. If it is not, it is not anything. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I respectfully suggest it is out of order.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to add too much to what has been said by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson). Undoubtedly the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is going to get into the discussion. I would say, in paraphrase of his words on Friday afternoon when Your Honour was considering another amendment, this is very cleverly worded. While the amendment of the other day dealt with something under the first three portions of the bill, which I have indicated on numerous occasions I do not feel is a money bill, this amendment deals entirely with part IV, which is definitely part of a money bill in the true sense of the word under the Old Age Security Act.
I would put it to Your Honour that while it is true the house may be vague in its amendments, yet this amendment is a complete nullity. Certainly the speakers from the party of the proposer of this amendment, and he himself, have indicated that the purpose of this is to discuss an increase in the old age security pension that will be payable. Certainly there would be no point in discussing a reduction. As the hon. member for Medicine Hat has said, one cannot do indirectly what he cannot do directly. I put it to Your Honour therefore that this amendment is highly dubious in so far as its regularity is concerned, in that all it asks is that the committee reconsider that basic amount of the old age security payment. However the committee cannot do anything to it, except perhaps to reduce the amount; yet the hon. member who has proposed this, has spoken only about an increase. He is only interested in an increase. I would very much doubt if this amendment is in order. I will not go into the other aspects that have been discussed or which may be discussed.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) began his remarks by saying that this amendment was, in effect, the same as the amendment which was proposed on Friday and which the Chair ruled out of order. I should like to point out there is one respect in which there is a vast difference between the two amendments. The
Canada Pension Plan
amendment proposed on Friday suggested that moneys be taken out of the Canada pension plan fund to pay old age security recipients and others, and this was in clear violation of the provisions of the resolution preceding the bill. The amendment that is now before you makes no such suggestion at all. The amendment that is now before you deals only with part IV of the bill, and more particularly with clause 120. I suggest that on that account it is quite different from the amendment proposed on Friday.
I should like to point out also that in the amendment on Friday there was virtually an instruction to the government to bring before a committee of the whole house a specific proposal including the precise amounts that were named. This amendment that is now proposed is not worded in that way at all. It does not make a specific proposal to the government. As a matter of fact, it does not even make a specific proposal to the committee of the whole. It is to the effect that the committee of the whole may reconsider one of the clauses, namely clause 120.
The hon. member for Medicine Hat and the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) as well, emphasized a point that a private member cannot move a motion that involves the expenditure of money. There is nobody in this house who does not realize that that is one of the basic rules of procedure of the House of Commons. No private member can move a motion that involves the expenditure of money. I submit that the motion now before the Chair, moved by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie), does not involve the expenditure of money. It does not even suggest what shall be done. The hon. member suggested in his speech what we think ought to be done, but what is before the house is a motion which would merely refer the bill back to the committee and give the committee of the whole the opportunity to reconsider the clause referred to and to decide at that point what to do. Let it be quite clear that if the government were unwilling at that point to present a royal recommendation for increasing expenditure, we would not be able to proceed any further; but I submit that if the house by a majority vote were to ask for this reference back, that would be a pretty clear indication to the government that the house did want action of this sort to be taken.
A point which was repeated several times by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. HOUSE OF COMMONS
Canada Pension Plan
Olson) was that it is a clear rule in this house that you cannot do indirectly what you are not able to do directly. That is a rule which is not stated in the books but it is frequently invoked. But may I also point out that this is precisely what private members do time and time again, particularly in the matter of private members' notices of motions which are put on the order paper. There is hardly a motion that a private member puts on the order paper which does not call for increased expenditure of some sort. A private member cannot move for the expenditure of money, so what does he do? He moves that in the opinion of this house the government should give consideration to making such and such an expenditure. Does the hon. member for Medicine Hat say that those motions are out of order or that they are improper? No doubt he has moved motions like that himself.
I would also point out, Mr. Speaker, that when the address or the budget is before us amendments are moved by all parties in opposition asking for changes which involve the expenditure of money. I am sure that my hon. friend has moved such an amendment or been party to one. I am referring to amendments which delete all the words after the word "that" and put in its place an expression to the effect that in the opinion of this house such and such should be done. As long as it is a statement of opinion that something should be done, it has been recognized over the years that that is not a violation of the principle that a private member cannot move something which involves the expenditure of money.
In effect, this amendment does precisely what a private member's notice of motion does. It does precisely what an amendment to the address or to the budget does. It expresses an opinion that we ought to go back to the committee of the whole for the purpose of reconsidering the amount of the old age security pension.
The only other thing I want to say, Mr. Speaker, is that the kind of amendment which my colleague the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond has moved is provided for in citation 415 of Beauchesne's fourth edition; and I may also say that there are many precedents which are almost exactly in the terms of this amendment. Let me read portions of citation 415:
(1) When a bill comes up for third reading a member may move that it be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole for the purpose of amending it in any particular.

Then there is paragraph (2):
Bills may be recommitted a number of times with or without limitation; in the latter case, the whole bill is opened to reconsideration, but in the former case the committee can only consider the clause or amendments or instructions referred to them.
In this case, the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond has moved an amendment that has a limitation spelled out in it. The limitation is that reconsideration be given at this point simply to clause 120. Paragraph (3) reads:
A bill may be recommitted, amended in committee, reported, considered on report and read a third time at the one sitting by simple order of the house.
There is a prohibition in the fourth paragraph of citation 415, which I read the other day, to the effect that an amendment to refer a bill back to the committee of the whole when the house is at third reading stage must not tend to change the principle approved on second reading. The other day I contended that that prohibition stood in the way of Friday's amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) because it did tend to change the principle of the Canada pension plan, from the plan that paid benefits to contributors to a plan which would pay benefits to non-contributors. This amendment, however, suggests no change in the principle approved on second reading. That principle, when it was passed on second reading, included part IV, which involved making certain changes in the Old Age Security Act. Mr. Speaker, I wish to deal very briefly with this point and to support the contention that the amendment moved by the hon. member is out of order. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) argued that this amendment made no specific proposal to the committee of the whole. The amendment asks for reconsideration of clause 120 of the bill, namely reconsideration of the basic amount of the old age security pension.
It is clear that there are several ways in which amendments can be made to a bill on third reading. One is to refer the bill back to a select committee. Another is to give it a three or a six months hoist. Another is to move a reasoned amendment. This amendment falls into none of these categories; it relies on a further method, namely referring part of the bill back to the committee of the whole.
I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that citation 415 of Beauchesne makes it perfectly clear that a motion of this kind must refer the bill back to the committee of the whole for the purpose of amending it in a particular. I suggest that the very virtue which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre found in his amendment destroys it, because a reference back must provide for a specific amendment to a clause of a bill. It is not sufficient to ask that the bill be reconsidered. If the hon. member refers to all the citations in Beauchesne he will find that in dealing with third readings of bills and in dealing with a reference back to the committee of the whole there are specific amendments to specific clauses. There has been no precedent brought forward by the hon. member which would suggest that a general reconsideration of this type is valid; the citation states quite clearly "for the purpose of amending it in any particular". Reconsidering the basic amount of the pension is very general, very philosophical. It is not amending the bill in any particular, which is a requirement of citation 415.
I suggest to Your Honour that you consider the amendment from another point of view. This amendment involves an instruction to the committee of the whole, and it is clear from the ruling made on Friday and the discussions which took place in the house that amendments of this kind are in effect instructions to the committee.
Canada Pension Plan
I should like to refer to citation 220 of Beauchesne's fourth edition which suggests that this amendment may be defective in another way.
Citation 220(2) reads in part:
" 'The principles which guide a limit in the system of instructions on going into committee may be thus stated: First, an instruction must empower the committee to do something which the committee is not otherwise empowered to do.-' "
Surely what the committee has done, and had full power to do, is consider the basic amount of the old age security pension. In support of the statement regarding the inadmissibility of this instruction, I should like to refer to May's seventeenth edition at page 544 which deals with instructions to committees. At that page under the heading "Inadmissible Instructions" is stated, in the second example under the subheading "Superfluous":
An instruction is superfluous and therefore out of order if it seeks to confer upon the committee power to make amendments in a bill which is already possessed by the committee under the provisions-
The committee of the whole had full opportunity and authority to discuss, and did discuss and decide, the basic amount of the old age security pension. It is my submission that the citation which I read from Beauchesne's fourth edition, supported by May's suggestion, gives a clear indication that this is an inadmissible instruction because it allegedly confers authority on the committee of the whole to do something which it has the authority to do and has in fact done.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, may I suggest that the intent of the hon. member is clear. He refrained from making any amendments during the consideration of this point by the committee of the whole. If this amendment was carried presumably we would go back in the committee of the whole to consideration of the basic amount. The hon. member would be unable to move any amendment at that time, just as he was unable to move an amendment during the committee of the whole consideration that has already taken place. The hon. member would be powerless to act and would achieve nothing by his amendment except a general discussion, which can take place on third reading. Therefore, any resort to recommittal is futile and would result in no conclusion, and would not provide a solution.
I suggest that on a common sense ground, and on grounds of logic, the house should not ask the committee to reconsider a matter

in respect of which no action is possible. If such action were to take place it would require a recommendation by the crown. This requirement prevented the hon. member from making any move on a procedural ground during the considerations of the committee of the whole.

Mr. Speaker, I am indeed pleased with your ruling that the amendment is in order. In effect it has the same result as the amendment we moved on Friday in that it provides a vehicle by which the house will again be allowed to consider the possibility of providing to recipients of old age security a more meaningful degree of assistance than is at present available, and from that point of view our attitude is not materially affected.
I want to indicate immediately that I will support the amendment in question and, indeed, will support any amendments forthcoming in the committee which will provide that our old age pensioners will receive a pension of $100 a month immediately. When one goes back to the latter part of 1963 and remembers how difficult it was to secure the increase of $10 which raised old age security to $75 a month, it is rather difficult to imagine

Canada Pension Plan
that the present government will agree to an amount of $100. However, in the circumstances I think we must face the fact that such an amount is in keeping with the facts of life today.
It is my hope that if we go back into committee on the bill we will be able to consider other aspects of the plan as well. In my view there are many problems facing our elder citizens that the plan as now conceived does not fully recognize. I believe that by increasing the amount of old age security we will correct the situation to a degree. Certainly the plan as now proposed has placed our elder citizens in a position where they think today that they are going to be beneficiaries, but the fact is they will realize in a very short period of time that they are not.
I also believe that the business of reducing the age of eligibility for old age security a year at a time until it is finally available at age 65 should be looked into again and, indeed, the age should be dropped to 65 immediately. Let us have none of this business of reducing it one year at a time. In line with the proposal presented by this party in committee, let us make old age security available immediately at age 65 and in the amount of $100 a month. Because of the insistence of the government to carry through with the plan as presently embodied in the bill, we are leading the elderly citizens of this nation down the garden path. During the election campaign they were told of the great benefits which would be made available to them when this plan came into effect, but under the terms of this bill they will be left out, forgotten, and in effect will have to live on what they presently receive, with the exception that their pension will be geared to the cost of living in a very nebulous way, one which resembles the $6 increase given to them in 1957 which was not sufficient to cover the cost of living increases they had to meet during the years prior to 1957.
I do not particularly care what method is adopted, or who proposes an amendment which is found to be in order. What I am concerned with is seeing that we get to the meat of the matter, to show the recipients of old age security, and those who will shortly be recipients, that we are willing to take their special situation into consideration.
I am pleased that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) was able to prepare an amendment that was found to be in order, and I am certainly going to support it. I am going to do what I can to assist the elderly citizens of our nation who

are meeting greater and greater difficulties because of the spiralling cost of living, a trend which will continue in the days ahead if the government is not willing to take greater action than it has indicated to date, with regard to those things which determine the cost of living.
When we reach the point where we take a vote on this matter I hope government members will also give consideration to the problems being faced by our elderly citizens. I hope government members will appreciate the fact that these people are not beneficiaries under this plan, will appreciate the fact that there will be real problems in trying to amend the bill once it becomes law, and will see to it that in the bill there is built-in protection for the recipients of old age security.
When this is done we can move forward and give consideration to adopting the bill, because we will know we will have looked after a great many Canadians who, today or in the near future, are or will become recipients of old age security, deserving of the minimum of $100 a month to maintain themselves with respect during the years ahead.

The council has recognized that a wage related contributory plan by its very nature tends to exclude certain groups of citizens from its protection; those person who are not attached to the labour market-widows with dependant children, the disabled-those who, while in the labour market, have very low or sporadic earnings and hence are unable to benefit very much or at all from the provisions of the plan; and those who are already retired.

In advancing the view that coverage be extended to the largest possible number, the council is expressing its conviction that public assistance programs should play a residual role rather than be used to meet the income-maintenance need of a large segment of the population. At the same time, the council recognizes the importance of public assistance in the total system of social security and argues as it did in 1958 that a new federal public assistance act is needed and that much greater attention must be paid to standards in public assistance, both in terms of administration and levels of benefits.

I now wish to quote briefly from the publication Commonwealth of March 24. Mr. Lemual Harris, N.D.P. member for Logan recently stated in the Manitoba legislature that the province had no provision for the rural poor. In his words:

I think I am qualified to speak for that generation of Canadians which, like myself, had a personal experience of pioneer life from the early days of this century. In fact, I may say I lived in a district where there was not a bathroom within a hundred miles. Those who worked in industry or in services have experienced years of low wages and poor working conditions; fortunately, those conditions have greatly improved since the

The producers provide knowledge, goods and services for the benefit of the community and the nation. Today we speak for the pioneer producers, the people ignored by this bill, the people who laid the foundations for our present development. Their efforts built schools, churches, hospitals and roads throughout Canada which now bring people and communities much closer together.

In conclusion, I must say that while national pension plans, national medicare and other socially desirable measures are necessary, we must at the same time realize that by these measures we are only laying a foundation for basic material security upon which we can then commence to build a civilization that will provide creative opportunities for our people. We must not forget that man does not live by bread alone. Even today some of our liberal intellectuals and labour leaders continue in the grip of the old spell in the belief that happiness can be found in economic security alone. In still stressing the first and unique importance of economic security, they are showing they do not recognize that this dream to many young people is no longer psychologically valid. They seem to continue to believe that we will automaticaly achieve our inalienable right to perpetual happiness when we are able to enjoy the benefits of complete economic security.
Canada Pension Plan
On the other hand, many people still believe that human dignity and happiness can only be achieved by the recreation of the good old days of self-reliance and competition between individuals and nations. However, we all know those days are gone forever. Human dignity cannot fully exist in the struggle to meet material needs nor can human dignity develop as the result of economic security alone. Genuine human dignity can only be created in a social environment of co-operation where the prime concern with consumption is replaced by the happiness that flows from co-operative creative activity. This approach to this problems means a great deal to many of our younger people across this country. Our people will respond to programs that provide an opportunity to use this cooperative creative activity in working for the development of world peace; in working for an opportunity to meet the material needs of those still destitute in other lands; in working for the participation of our people to meet the problems of our own country, including the problems of automation, unemployment and other related problems.
For this purpose, Mr. Speaker, we must bend every effort toward the building of a united Canada. I am on very sound ground now, Mr. Speaker, because I wish to conclude by quoting from a broadcast made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) on April 23, 1963. I should like to conclude by quoting his challenging remarks on that occasion;
The task ahead then is immense but it is not frightening. It is complex beyond simple description but it is not impossible. It will not be an easy time, but it will, I pledge you, be a time to excite the daring, to test the strong and to give new promise to the timid. It will indeed be a time of direction and decision, where our efforts are sustained, our purpose clear and our faith high.
We trust the members of the government, Mr. Speaker, will approach this amendment in the spirit exemplified by the Prime Minister when he spoke on that occasion. I should like first, Mr. Speaker, to thank the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) for congratulating me upon my patience during the long consideration of this bill-or perhaps my impatience. I was not sure which phrase referred to me or if both did. However, at this stage, with this amendment moved, I believe it has become

Canada Pension Plan
obvious to everyone that neither the Conservative party, the New Democratic party nor the Creditistes want to see a wage related pension plan in Canada. I believe this bill has spent as much time in committee as any other bill in recent times. The ideas which have been put forward by the Conservative party in an amendment which was ruled out of order on Friday, and now by the New Democratic party in an amendment which was ruled in order, referred to matters which received long and careful study during the 21 days that this bill was considered in committee of the whole, as well as in the special committee which had 51 sittings to hear evidence. The special committee brought forward recommendations to this house, most of which were adopted by the government.
The amendment of the New Democratic party refers this bill back to committee for reconsideration of a matter which was considered by the committee. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said he could not move an amendment which would achieve his purpose and therefore asked the government to move an amendment to increase the old age security pension to $100 per month. The hon. member did this in committee of the whole, so all he is hoping to achieve by this amendment, apparently, is a further delay in proceedings by referring it back to committee of the whole after we have spent such a long time considering the bill and after the government has spent some time considering this matter. He wants the government to say exactly the same thing as it said when the bill was in committee of the whole when this particular question was raised.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not think this can be looked upon as anything but delay and filibuster tactics on the part of-

-the Conservative party and the New Democratic party, who obviously do not want a Canada pension plan. I believe the Creditistes have at least been honest: They have come out and said they do not want the Canada pension plan in its present form. They wasted several days in the committee debate to impress upon everybody that they did not want a Canada pension plan, and stated their reasons, and then we moved into third reading.
I cannot help but think that the official opposition and the New Democratic party sat back and gloated while they wasted the time of the committee, knowing that on a vote the

New Democratic party or the Conservative party would not dare vote against the Canada pension plan. Through the action which has been taken by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), he is obviously trying to kill the Canada pension plan by sending it back to the committee and opening a matter of debate which has already been decided. As indicated by the hon. member of the official opposition who spoke a few minutes ago, when they get back into committee they do not want to talk about the particular subject matter raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre; they want to talk about all the other aspects of the Canada pension plan. In effect, what the official opposition and the New Democratic party are trying to do is to create a merry-go-round which never comes to a stop, so that the people of Canada never get a Canada pension plan.
I could not let this point go past, Mr. Speaker, without once more reiterating a few of the statements which I made when the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre suggested, as was his right, in the committee of the whole that the Canada pension plan payment be increased to $100 at age 65. He knew that he could not move this in committee of the whole, but it was discussed. He now wants to go back to the committee of the whole to discuss it again. I pointed out at that time to the members of the committee exactly what would be the estimate of cost to the people of Canada if this were done. Let us not assume that these are costs to the government of Canada; they are costs to the people of Canada. Because the only way the old age security pension can be provided, as indicated both in the bill and in the old age security legislation, is out of taxes raised for that specific purpose. The additional cost to pay $100 a month at age 65 would be, as I mentioned, $810 million. This is almost double the present cost of the old age security pensions in Canada.
Let us just think what that would mean for the taxpayers of this country. It would mean virtually doubling the taxes presently levied on the taxpayers to support the old age security pension. I have made a calculation, for which only I accept responsibility- it has not been checked by the Department of Finance-that on the same basis of taxation-that is, increasing personal income tax to a maximum of $120 and increasing sales tax and corporation income tax-it would cost the average taxpayer earning $4,000 a year $210 per year in additional taxation.

The New Democratic party, which is supposed to be the party in support of labour in this country, now turns around and says: Certainly, we are quite willing to increase the taxes of the average wage earner in this country by $210 a year in order that we may have old age pensions at age 65 of $100 a month. I doubt whether the man earning $4,000 a year in Canada today would be willing to stand for this kind of action. If this is the kind of action proposed by the New Democratic party, I think I would be very pleased to see them vote in favour of this kind of tax increase which would affect every workingman in this country.
