speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have before us an amendment which asks that Bill No. C-136 be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole house for the purpose of reconsidering the basic amount of the old age security pension, as set out in clause 120. I know that Your Honour has ruled this amendment to be in order, but I am very concerned about what we are going to do with Bill No. C-136 if we do get back into committee of the whole house to reconsider clause 120. Because obviously there is no possibility of any private member or any member of this house, other than a minister of the crown, moving an amendment to clause 120 which would in fact increase the basic amount of the old age security pension; and in the debate which we have had thus far the amount suggested is $100 a month. So that leaves the members of this house, if they want to follow the rules which ought to be followed, with only one alternative, one course of action, and that is to use the time allotted for debate to try to impress upon the government that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) should come back to this house with a resolution or amendment which would give effect to this suggested increase.
So, Mr. Speaker, in spite of the objections that were raised as to the propriety of this amendment, I would suggest that at this stage this is the only avenue open to us.
We in this party have long advocated that the basic amount of the old age security pension should be substantially higher than it has been in the past, and is now. I say that because I think that there is a fairly sound argument economically to support the contention that it would be desirable in Canada to have a higher old age security pension. The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) has suggested that it is going to cost some-
Canada Pension Plan
thing like $810 million to change the basic amount of the old age security pension at age 65 from $75 to $100 a month.
I should like to remind him that it may well be that there would be an expenditure of this particular amount if the Old Age Security Act were amended accordingly. But I would also suggest, Mr. Speaker, that there are other expenditures of the federal government, large expenditures, which would be lessened to a considerable degree if in fact the old age pension was increased. For example, we know that there are a large number of senior citizens who find themselves unable to cope with the cost of living on a mere $75 a month. These people are therefore obliged to seek income from other sources. In many cases this is done by retaining jobs and positions in our economy from which under other circumstances they would have retired.
In addition, during the past number of years there has been a tremendous expenditure through the unemployment insurance commission to provide for the unemployed people in our economy. We know, for example, that in 1957 there were $920 million odd in the unemployment insurance fund which during the following four years was completely dissipated. Over and above that there were other substantial payments or grants or loans made by the federal government to this fund.
It seems to me that if we were to increase the basic amount of the old age security pension it would be possible for some of our senior citizens to retire from jobs which they are now obliged to retain in spite of their advancing years. If this were done it would open up an opportunity for the younger people to take on some of these vacated jobs. I suggest it also follows that there would be a substantial decrease in the amount of money required to sustain the unemployment insurance commission payments. So that the figure of $810 million advanced by the Minister of National Revenue, while that may be the expenditure under the particular act, is not a true reflection of the cost to the federal treasury because there could be savings made in other areas.
There is one other very interesting point that ought to be mentioned, Mr. Speaker. If one reads financial newspapers today he will see opinions advanced almost daily to the effect that one of the main props supporting Canada's buoyant economy is the level of consumer spending. Every single dollar increase in the old age pensioners' income in this country will immediately find its way

Canada Pension Plan
into additional consumer spending and thereby increase the whole level of economic activity which, as we all know, results in an increase in revenue to the government. For that reason, in addition to the others I have advanced, the $810 million figure does not truly represent the balance of cost to the government.
In some respects we have recognized, but only partially, that consumer spending on the part of recipients of the old age security pension would strengthen the prop to the buoyancy of Canada's economy. The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) has suggested that all things are contained in the amendment; but very clearly they are not. The amendment simply suggests that we refer this back to the committee. I hope that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) can be persuaded to bring forth an amendment to clause 120 which will give effect to some of the things suggested in respect of sending the bill back to the committee. Otherwise there is really no possible benefit which can be achieved by supporting the amendment.
There are several other clauses in Bill C-136 which ought to be reconsidered. I can assure the house that I have long been an advocate of a portable pension plan for Canadians which would allow earned pension benefits, including employer contributions and pension fund earnings, to remain with the individual who earned them even though he changed his job. All Canadians should have the opportunity to participate in a Canada pension plan, whether they belong to a large or small payroll group, or are self-employed. The bill as it now stands does not in my view provide the kind of universal contributory pension plan which would in fact give effect to those things I have mentioned.
There are a number of very complex clauses that deal with what is called an earnings related pension scheme. We have this matter of maximum contributions related to what might be termed net income during certain years, referred to in clause 16. Clause 20 refers to a pension index, and clause 21 refers to an earnings index. As far as I am concerned, income is clearly defined at the present time by the Income Tax Act, and we do not need all this complexity in arriving at what an employee, or any Canadian, may have earned by way of pension benefit. It seems to me that we could have a far more effective and simple bill to meet the needs of Canadians who do not now have access to pension funds, by simply relating the contributions to the

benefits within the scope or limit of both a minimum and maximum, basing the contributions very easily on an option clause. I am not suggesting that it would be possible to have a universal pension plan without adopting some minimum contribution related to earnings, nor am I suggesting that there should not be a maximum. However, we must realize that self-employed individuals particularly have irregular levels of net income. If during the period of years used to establish benefits payable under a Canada pension plan to a self-employed individual he has received a low level of earnings, under the provisions of Bill C-136 he would be prevented from earning maximum benefits under the plan as it now stands.
I suggest that perhaps half of the Bill C-136 could be eliminated by relating the benefits to contributions, leaving some options in so far as the amount of contribution is concerned. I hope there will be some amendments suggested by the minister, even if not this year, which will simplify this plan so that benefits can be directly related to contributions, and so the contributions can be based on an option within limits imposed by a minimum and a maximum.
We need a universal contributory pension plan in Canada. Every Canadian, no matter whom he works for, or whether he is selfemployed, should have the opportunity to earn benefits under such a plan. The plan now before us for consideration is so complex and restrictive as to the amount of contribution that can be made, and as to the benefits that can be earned, that in my opinion it is a long way from being something that could be called a universal contributory pension plan.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) have repeatedly tried to explain this earnings related pension benefit part of the plan. We have had some argument as to whether the plan is actuarially sound, although the minister has continually stated that it is. If the plan is in fact actuarially sound, then there is no valid reason that any Canadian should be prevented from making contributions in excess of 3.6 per cent of net income, if he so chooses, up to a predetermined maximum.
Mr. Speaker, those are a few of the comments I wanted to make before this plan becomes law. Whether or not we reconsider clause 120 is something the house will decide in a few minutes. I hope the minister will be prepared to come forward with an amend-

ment which will give effect to a change in the basic amount of old age security pensions. Whether she does or not, I hope she will give some serious reconsideration to the tremendous complexities of this plan in an attempt to develop something which might be truthfully and properly referred to as a universal contributory pension plan to which all Canadians from all parts of our economic structure will have access, with the opportunity of contracting for the amount of pension benefits they wish to earn.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, because I think it is necessary to retain some direction in connection with our debates and proceedings, I must say that I hope there will be some action taken with respect to clause 120 if it goes back to the committee. Certainly I must agree that there was a rather extended study of the matter when the bill was in committee of the whole, but supporting this amendment will be nothing but an exercise in futility unless the government comes forward with some kind of an amendment of its own. We know very well that no private member of the house can move such an amendment. Therefore if the bill does go back to the committee we will look forward to receiving notice from the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) that the government is prepared to make substantial amendments to clause 120.

I did not want to be that rude. Throughout the entire consideration of the bill the government has been impatient to move along with it and has taken a dogmatic attitude with regard to not considering any changes suggested by the opposition. It is this attitude which is the reason that we are in the position in which we find ourselves at this time.
We have a very peculiar situation. First of all, and I regret this for the second or third time, the members who sit to our immediate left could have endeavoured to secure a similar result by voting for our amendment; but instead, they voted against our amendment the other day. Now, however, they are proposing something similar by way of an amendment. The hon. member for Medicine 20220-817
Canada Pension Plan
Hat (Mr. Olson) endeavoured to show that the amendment was out of order, but at the same time supported it. He also said it might be an exercise in futility and, as I suggested a few moments ago, I agree.
The government's position in this regard has been altogether too adamant and too dictatorial. They must realize that the move they made in order to make pensions payable at age 65 was agreed to by all members of the house. When the Minister of National Revenue suggests that we are filibustering against a wage related pension plan I would have him understand first and foremost that he is wrong. I will not say that the members of our party will vote 100 per cent in favour of the bill, but their vote will not be far from being unanimous and will indicate where we stand in this regard when the vote is taken.
The Minister of National Revenue also mentioned the heavy burden that would be placed on people earning $4,000 to $5,000 so far as taxes are concerned if the amendment now before us were implemented. I suggest that the situation is a peculiar one. In the bill as it now stands the exemptions are $600 for the employed person and $800 for the self-employed person. I suggest right away that this is one area where the government has been very remiss. If they had only seen fit to set the exemption level at $1,200 or $1,500 across the board they would have been doing something very valuable for the country. But they know that in the field of agriculture particularly their policy is wrong, and that net incomes in some cases are considerably below such a figure. I suggest to the Minister of National Revenue that he should investigate the possibility of raising the exemption level. I heard him make the comment the other evening that this was something toward which we should move and I suggest it is the correct and proper thing to do. The exemption level should be raised considerably.
With circumstances such as they are in Canada today, surely we should not have any great number of Canadians who are in this position. Yet we know this is the case. This is what I was trying to say the other night, and I am glad you are allowing me these few minutes to put these matters on the record, Mr. Speaker, because it is the last time I will have the opportunity to speak. I was amazed to find that a recent survey conducted in an area of the province of Ontario indicated that in some cases net incomes were a minus figure. They were not $600 or $800. These two figures are also rather perplexing because as soon as the self-employed man,

Canada Pension Plan
which I am, makes $801 he is taxable for an additional $201. I believe I am right in my statement. That too is a very peculiar situation.
Let us not be deceived as to the position we find ourselves in this afternoon. I intend to support the amendment, but I am only voting for it because I am in favour of the end result. That is more than the members of the N.D.P. were when our amendment was before the house. Therefore I suggest to the house they must have some other motive for moving this amendment. Maybe they are against a wage related plan. I do not know; but I am not. The area of responsibility about which the Minister of National Revenue spoke falls directly on the shoulders of the government. He mentioned this the other evening when we were discussing this very point. His position is a valid one, but when the government takes the adamant and dictatorial attitude that they will not consider anything emanating from the opposition, how else can we move? If he says we are irresponsible, then he had better find out what the old people of the country are thinking today.
One member to my left made the point that this money would be put into circulation immediately and would increase consumer spending. I believe that to be correct. I do not think any member of the house deals with more welfare cases in his constituency than I do, and I find in each and every case that even such an amount of money is not too much if one has to exist on it. It is an easy thing for members of the government party to shrug off this matter and there is no doubt they are going to vote solidly in a block. You can bet your last nickel on that. The whip will be out and they will have no alternative but to vote against the amendment. In other words, there is not one drop of the milk of human kindness left in the hearts of those members who support the government.
When the statement is made that consumer spending would be increased, that is certainly true. So far as any burden that might be created is concerned it does not matter whether it is covered by the Canada pension plan or by other taxation. The fact is that these people need the money. From correspondence that arrived in my office this morning I can show you that these people need additional funds. Of course, something might be done in the field of old age assistance. I am not familiar with the plans of other provinces but in the province of Ontario there are supplementary benefits for medical

care and so on, but people are not totally covered.
It seems to me that the government is trying to restrict their plan because the next carrot they will hold out will probably be a medicare plan or maybe another $25 at some future time. But if they want to act in a responsible way they will agree to an increase in old age security while we are considering this plan. They will do so while this plan is under discussion. If the minister is prepared to introduce an amendment of that sort he will find that we will support the bill and maybe even pass it this evening. That is my attitude at least, and I am sure I can convince my colleagues to do the same. May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

When the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) talked about delaying the passage of this legislation I should like to remind you, sir, that it was held up for five days because this government was so inefficient that it did not even have the evidence translated and printed in French.
These are the people who now object to our party introducing a simple amendment dealing with a point which we think is of great importance. These are the people who held up the whole business of passing this legislation for five days because of their failure to carry out the ordinary procedure of translating the evidence. As a matter of fact the amendment which has been produced by my hon. friend from Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie) does not deal with the Canada pension plan at all; it deals with the old age security pension, and the fact that the legislation we are now being asked to pass does nothing at all for the hundreds of thousands of people who are at present retired and who will get no benefit whatsoever from the Canada pension plan. The minister said this afternoon we were endeavouring to kill this plan. I should like to point out that this party probably more than any party in Canada popularized the idea of a portable pension plan in this country.
At the convention in 1961 we outlined such a plan in two parts, one part to take care of those who would contribute over the years and who would be entitled to a retirement pension, and the other part to deal with those who had already retired or who would retire before the full benefits of this pension were available to them. While the Canada pension plan will be of some assistance in providing adequate security for those who can benefit from it, it is not designed to help those who have already retired. When the minister is so foolhardy as to suggest we are trying to kill the pension plan I would say to him that my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. MARCH 29, 1965
Knowles) probably knows as much about this plan as anybody on the other side, if not more, and has worked harder than anybody in this house to get this legislation passed.
The hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. *Winkler) has just said that we failed to support the Conservative amendment. The reason has been made clear. We refused to do so because in our opinion it would undermine the Canada pension plan. As we made clear in the convention of 1961 setting out our ideas, we thought the Canada pension plan should stand on its own feet, that it should be designed to help those who contribute to it and therefore assistance to those unable to benefit under the plan should come by way of old age security legislation.
I can understand the Minister of National Revenue being in a temper this afternoon. Whenever the Liberals fail to get their own way, whenever members of the house are not prepared to rush in and vote for anything the government puts before them they are accused of filibustering and obstruction. The fact is members opposite do not want it drawn to the attention of the people of Canada just how shabbily they are treating the old people of this country. This government ought to be ashamed of the treatment it is meting out to the old people of Canada who have to live on nothing else but their old age pensions. A pension of $75 a month with the cost of living where it is today, having risen by more than one third since 1949, is completely inadequate to maintain even a minimum standard of decency for these older people. That is why the government wants this rushed through.

We have said repeatedly that we think 25 per cent of the average earnings of the participants is too low; it is certainly lower than Liberal promises prior to the election. But the one group which has not been dealt with at all is the group consisting of old age pensioners who have already retired or who will not be eligible for benefits. That is why this amendment has been moved.
The Minister of National Revenue has once again built his whole case on the statement that we cannot afford to raise the old age security pension to, let us say, $100 a month. This is the song we have heard from the minister again and again. He will be known as "we-can't-afford-it Benson" if he keeps this up for long. The minister does not say, of course, that we cannot afford to spend $1,550 million a year on defence. A return which has been made to the house shows that since the end of the war we have spent $22.5 billion on defence. The minister does not suggest we cannot afford that. But he says we cannot afford to raise the pensions of those 65 and over to $100 a month.
He goes on to give some strange reasons. He says it would mean the taxation of the workers. It is rather characteristic of the pattern of thinking of a Liberal government that whenever they think about taxes, they think about taxes on workers. That was shown by the fact that when this pension

Canada Pension Plan
plan was introduced it called for a premium of 1 per cent because it was to be a pay as you go pension plan. However, in the process of negotiations with the provinces the premium has been raised to 1.8 per cent and it is now a partially funded plan. The workers of this country and the employers are going to pay one third more than they really need to pay in order to supply social capital for the provinces. I do not for one moment object to raising social capital for the provinces, but I say that if we require social capital for the provinces there are better ways to get it than by taxing people of $5,000 a year and less. If the government want to raise capital, then there are those in higher income brackets who could afford to pay very generously toward providing social capital for the provinces. But the government's thinking always follows the lines of, "How can you tax workers?"
Let me suggest to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) that he could raise the money to increase the old age pension to $100 a month at 65 years of age by taxing some of his friends. There are certain places where he might get this $820 million which he says it will cost. For instance, he could take the ceiling off the 4 per cent income tax charge on incomes. At the present time the old age security tax of 4 per cent is only levied on the first $3,000 of taxable income. The minister could take the ceiling off. There is no reason why those with large incomes could not contribute to providing security to the older people in this country. Did that ever occur to the minister? Did it ever occur to the minister that he could also raise the old age security tax from 3 per cent to 4 per cent on corporations? The personal income tax levy for old age security purposes has been raised to 4 per cent; there is no reason why the tax on corporations could not also be raised to 4 per cent.
One can hardly pick up a financial paper these days but one finds corporation after corporation reporting increased profits. Here is the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company reporting profits of $39,136,000 for 1964-up 31 per cent. B.C. Forest Products, profits up 27.3 per cent. One might go on with the long list. Profits have never been higher in the history of Canada than they were in 1964. Did it ever occur to the minister that if he needs revenue from which to pay higher pensions to the old people of this country, the tax on profits could be increased? Has the minister given any thought to a capital gains tax in this country? If we are

going to tax people who make $3,000, $4,000 and $5,000 a year, as we do, and tax people who make this money by the sweat of their brow, is there any reason why we should not tax people who make tens of thousands of dollars from land speculation and from playing the stock market?

The Hall commission report on health services has two very excellent chapters in which they project the possibilities for economic growth in this country from 1961 to 1991. They point out that for every percentage point that we can reduce unemployment, we will increase the gross national product of Canada by over $4 billion annually. About a quarter of this will find its way in various forms back into the federal treasury. The government of Canada can finance this $820 million account to which the minister has referred by promoting sufficient economic growth so that we can reduce unemployment by one percentage point. If we can reduce it by two percentage points, we can finance not only an increase

in old age pensions but go a long way toward financing a medicare program as well. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, there is no better way to stimulate economic growth than to put purchasing power into the pockets of these old people who would be the main beneficiaries of raising the pension to $100 a month.
The economic council of Canada have pointed out that the greatest lack in our economy today is the lack of effective demand; and if we are to have effective demand then purchasing power must be put into the pockets of those who will buy consumer goods. There is no group more likely to spend income on the purchase of consumer goods than these people of 65 years of age and over. I doubt if there is anything the government could do that would stimulate and promote growth more rapidly than to increase the old age pension, as we have suggested, to $100 a month and make it payable at 65 years of age.
It is not my intention to hold up the passage of this legislation, Mr. Speaker, but I want to point out that the members of this party have promoted the idea of a Canada pension plan. Canada Pension Plan
I do not think the Minister of National Revenue was right in saying that the three days spent in clearly expressing our views on Bill No. C-136 in the house were a waste of time. I find it rather strange that when we were called upon, last Thursday, to consider an amendment to refer back the bill to the committee of the whole in order to reconsider the basic amount of the old age pension, although the house had already been in committee of the whole for the past 21 days, the press as well as television and radio news bulletins were all pointing out that the matter was urgent and that the house had wasted 21 days on Bill No. C-136.
As a matter of fact, those who introduced an amendment last Friday were the first ones to ask us, last Thursday, to pass the bill as quickly as possible. It was urgent.
Today government members are saying it is urgent while those on this side of the house suggest it is no longer so. In fact, last Friday afternoon was spent in discussing whether the proposed amendment was out of order or not, the final vote being taken at five o'clock.
The amendment now before us bears a strange resemblance to that of last Friday, designed to send the bill back to committee.
The previous speaker referred a while ago to the tremendous job the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) had done to promote the passing of Bill No. C-136. I know he certainly co-operated closely with the government to have the motion for second reading passed. As a matter of fact, everything possible was done to prevent a motion from being discussed during the question period, precisely to hasten the passing of the motion for second reading. And now we are going to start discussing all over again, for a week's time, whether or not the bill should go back to committee.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether there is not a game of cat and mouse going on by way of points of order to find out how political capital can be made. In fact, the purpose seems to be to use the motion on third reading to urge the government to increase the basic pension to $100 per month through an amendment to clause 120.
I think it would also have been proper last week to allow us to put forward all the arguments that were referred to in relation to the amendments moved last Friday and this afternoon.
When the house was in committee, I pointed out several times that it might be an error to adopt the fourth part that was annexed

Canada Pension Plan
to Bill No. C-136 and that it could be misleading for the public concerning old age pensions.
I do not think that the matter is being made clearer. In fact, it is more confused than ever. Judging from remarks by Conservative and government members and from what the previous speaker was saying a while ago, there is not so much urgency.
In July 1963, a resolution concerning the adoption of a compulsory pension plan was brought before the house. This is now March 1965 and I think it can truly be said that we do have a stable government in the sense that it stays put, going neither forward nor backward, but always staying at the same spot. Such a state of affairs has been going on for two years.
Three babies were presented to us with regard to the old age pension and now on the motion for third reading, having passed hastily the motion for second reading, they want the bill to be referred back to the committee. Are we being serious or not?
Those who moved an amendment last week claimed that it was possible, out of the contributions paid under the first three parts of the bill, to increase the amount from $75 to $100. At that time, we abstained from voting. We were left free to vote or not, according to our conscience, even if we were in the house.
We did not fall into that trap. We feel that it is a mistake to include part IV in Bill No. C-136. The proposed amendment requests that the bill be sent back to the committee in order to study again a possible amendment to clause 120 to change the basis of the pensions under old age security. Not only was it considered previously by the committee but it prompted a second resolution. It was found that Bill No. C-136 could include all the possible judicial and legal responsibilities from the constitutional point of view, with regard to the province of Quebec or other provinces, which are empowered to legislate in the field of social security. Finally the bill was completed by adding part IV to it.
It is proposed to go back to the committee now that this has been approved on second reading. Yet, when the opposition asks for a revision of the basic old age pension, under social security, hon. members opposite answer by quoting figures like $821 million.
The hon. member who spoke before me gave figures which bear repeating.
It was stated that since 1945, nearly $22 billion were allocated for defence in peace-

time. It could also be pointed out that the blue book which was tabled last week does not seemingly call for any great reduction of defence expenditures, even though we are still at peace.
In my opinion, the senior citizens who would greatly benefit if they were to get old age pensions of $100 instead of $75 would not feel too kindly toward the Liberal party if they heard that national defence appropriations in peacetime were not reduced by a single cent even but that, for lack of funds, they will be deprived of such an increase.
An increase in old age pensions would cost $821 million. At once, they hasten to say that new taxes would have to be established. They never admit that it is the financial system which compels the Minister of National Health and Welfare as well as the Minister of National Revenue to take $5 out of Peter's pocket to give it to Paul. They will not admit it. This is a real compulsion system.
Of the four ministers who will have to administer this bill, none will get money elsewhere than in the pockets of the taxpayer every time a step forward is taken in the field of social security.
If war broke out tomorrow morning, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of National Revenue as well as the Minister of Finance or the other ministers would not wonder if we should make our war effort, as long as we would have materials, natural resources and unemployed who would then have no more problems. There would be no financial objection to our participation in world carnage, as it happened in the past.
But when it comes to increasing by $25 a month a pension consistent with the needs of people 65 years and over in this country, they invoke all the fiscal arguments, those dictated beforehand by finance to the Minister of National Revenue and to the Minister of Finance.
I pity the Minister of National Health and Welfare who is caught in that strait-jacket. If, with all the generosity in the world, she would commiserate with older people and allow those people who gave 30 or 40 years of their life to their country, to have a little comfort in this century of plenty, she would be caught between a Minister of Finance and a Minister of National Revenue who would cut down her ambitions, because we are always restricted.
The amendment now before us asks that the whole question be referred to the committee. I am not against the bill being re-

ferred back to the committee, and I must say I shall vote for this amendment, but not before proposing a subamendment which, I hope, will give cause for reflection to some of those who would not understand at the proper time, when we were already in committee and should have taken all the time required to study part IV of Bill C-136.
This amendment prompts the Minister of National Revenue to ask himself: Where will the money come from? We shall have to increase some taxes that taxpayers will be unable to bear.
Always the same arguments.
Some will no doubt say that we always put forward the same arguments ourselves, but it is because it is just as true today as it was yesterday.
Governments are restricted by the financial system which entirely controls them in the sphere of security as well as in other areas.
A moment ago I said that should a war break out, we could obtain the few billions of dollars required. But we cannot obtain the few billions necessary to assist persons who have reached the age of 65 and who cannot afford to live decently, who cannot pay for the medical care their health requires, who, in many cases, cannot pay the cost of decent housing, lead a modest family life, between father and mother, without being dependant on the son-in-law, the daughter or the son.
We are restricted; we have no funds unless we dig deeper into the taxpayers' pockets.
If there is a field where the state should assume its responsibilities, it is precisely that of social security, and this, in a suppletory role acknowledged by every political philosophy of the world; the government should certainly play a suppletory part from time to time, if necessary, but not carry out a complete substitution, as in Bill No. C-136. It should only meet the needs of those unable to obtain by themselves the money required to manage their own affairs and profit as much as possible from the abundant resources of their country.
Material resources are not lacking in our country to bring security to older citizens while respecting their freedom.
Goodwill or outside pressure in favour of a revision of the pension plan are surely not lacking.
I am just about sure that if a free vote were taken in the house on the advisability of increasing to $100 a month the pension of people 65 and over, 99 per cent of hon. members would be in favour of such a boost, if 20220-818
Canada Pension Plan
they voted according to their conscience. However, the vote will again go along party lines; once again, it will reflect the dictum of finance.
Who runs this country? Is it this parliament of 265 members or the financiers, those controllers of the economic blood of our nation who ration the purchasing power of the aged?
People of 65 or older surely have a right to some control through us and they need better understanding from their leaders if they are to enjoy a little welfare in such a rich country as Canada.
Why not admit the possibility of getting the necessary funds to enable the state to play its supplementary role, by participating directly though new credits secured from the Bank of Canada to increase the consuming power of those people, which will do nothing worse-as stated a little earlier by the hon. member who spoke before me-than increase productivity in the next five or ten years, not to mention that this will also increase the purchasing power of the people who will benefit from that increased pension?
It must be remembered that at the present time a great number of people get social security or an old age pension, but that a large number of them are almost regularly short of money before the end of the month or the arrival of their cheque.
It means that this would simply increase the consuming power; thus, the consuming power of those people being increased, by the same token productivity is increased, which is a policy more in keeping with the needs of the people than that which today is only concerned with creating needs through advertising. This would allow people with needs to be met at this time to buy the products they require not through advertising, but to order basic things, such as medical care, adequate food, adequate housing, adequate clothing.

Mr. Speaker, before the final vote on third reading on Bill No. C-136 is taken we feel that there is one remaining issue with which the house should deal. That issue has to do with the date at which age 65 as the new eligible age for old age security is to come into effect. We did deal with this matter when we were in committee of the whole. As a matter of fact, on March 15, as recorded at page 12379 of Hansard, there were two standing votes in committee on this question. In one instance we on this side lost by a vote of 86 to 51. A few minutes later we lost by a vote of 87 to 52.
We in this party, Mr. Speaker, feel that the house should deal with this question, and we can deal with it very simply. Clause 119 of the bill specifies that the qualifying age for the old age security pension is 65. That provision in clause 119 is qualified, however, by the provision of clause 122, which stipulates that for the next few years persons under 70 will not get the old age security pension except on the basis of the eligible age coming down a year at a time. This matter can be taken care of very simply. All that needs to be done is for clause 122 to be voted down in committee of the whole. If that is to be done the bill will have to be referred back to the committee of the whole for the purpose of reconsidering clause 122.
Therefore, in a minute or so I shall propose just such an amendment. I make it clear that what we are asking for is that the house support the principle that the government has accepted, namely that the old age security pension should be paid at age 65. But we ask that instead of the full implementation of this provision having to wait until 1970, it be given immediate effect upon the final approval of Bill C-136, which we hope is now imminent.
As we pointed out when we were debating this matter in committee of the whole, the government itself has found it possible to provide for the full pension of $75 a month to be paid at ages below 70, without any increase in taxation. The increase which was enacted two years ago in order to pay an additional $10 by way of old age security has been found to be sufficient to pay the $75 a month on a sliding scale down to age 65 by 1970. We feel that by a further sharpening
[Mr. Ouellet.l
of pencils and by looking at such methods as those suggested a few moments ago when the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) argued for the pension to be raised to $100 a month, this provision could be altered and the old age security pension, which is going to be effective at age 65 in five years, could become effective at that age right away.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, this matter has been fully argued. There were votes on it in committee of the whole, but not all hon. members were here for those votes. More of them are here tonight and we think that this is the place where the decision should be made. Therefore, since no further argument is necessary, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett):

maintopic: POWER-BRITISH COLUMBIA-FISH PROTECTION IN DAM CONSTRUCTION
POWER-BRITISH COLUMBIA-FISH PROTECTION IN DAM CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can well understand everybody's anxiety to get home. However, on March 25 I asked a question of the Minister of Fisheries on behalf of the united conservation front for Kootenay West which includes members supporting all parties and numerous organizations. I asked the question with the knowledge of the responsibility of the federal government for the protection of the commercial and sport fisheries in Canada. Rod and gun clubs, chambers of commerce and other groups are concerned about the danger of the possible extinction of the fish population of the Arrow lakes and other areas affected by the building of the High Arrow, Mica and Duncan dams as the result of the clearing of the basins according to the policy announced by the B.C. hydro and power authority.
My question to the minister was: Would the minister inform the house if he is aware of

this situation and what action the federal government intends to take to make certain that the fish population of these waters is conserved? This is a very serious situation, Mr. Speaker, and I shall quote briefly from a resolution passed by the Nelson rod and gun club which has been endorsed by other organizations, including chambers of commerce and so on:
Whereas the four major dams, namely, Arrow, Mica creek, Duncan and Libby in the Columbia project are contained in areas having a recreational potential of inestimable value, and
Whereas water storage areas to be created by the four dams will, when full, be of great depth* steep banks, scrubby and timbered shorelines;
Whereas water reservoirs resulting from said dams are designed to flood thousands of acres of farm land, range land, low lands, camping grounds, beaches, sport fish spawning beds, and
Whereas notwithstanding propaganda to the contrary we cannot agree that these affected areas will be enhanced to the degree of enchantment which will attract thousands of tourists, conversely, we predict a substantial loss of camping, holidaying and outdoor hunting and fishing types, and
Whereas, acknowledging the inclusion of a hydro electric installation in the Mica Creek dam, which will provide a small labour team with employment after completion, the Duncan, Arrow and Libby dams will have nothing to offer area employment, other than that required for nominal unkeep. In retrospect, an enormous potential in recreational values in the depopulated areas will be destroyed, the few people required for maintenance will do little to increase district economy.
Whereas, history and scientific knowledge has proven that, regardless of relentless restocking programs, fish rehabilitation requires at least 20 years to establish and in many known projects never succeeds and without complete scientific facts to prove why, uncleaned reservoirs present the greatest resistance to sport fish rehabilitation, and
Whereas all facts point decisively to the necessity of full scale reservoir clearing preceding flooding because,
A.	Areas affected will require rehabilitation as rapidly as possible to bolster their economy.
B.	The multiple use and protection of all air, land and water resources must reconcile the demands of an exploding population and economy. We the people, represented by those we elect to govern purport to adhere to this factual philosophy and
Whereas in 1961, and before ratification of the Columbia River Treaty, the west Kootenay rod and gun clubs zone prepared a brief which in no way opposed the building of dams but took a reasonable approach to the inevitable "march of progress." The brief gave a complete coverage of all aspects for the protection, conservation, propagation, rehabilitation of fish and wildlife and the necessary allied recreational facilities if and when dams and resulting reservoirs were constructed. The brief contained recommendations resulting from scientific data obtained from similar projects which by virtue of man's errors and mistakes in his efforts to simulate nature, assisted the authors of the brief in resolving their conclusions and recommendations. The brief was accepted, by the government and sportsmen alike, as the most comprehensible, intelligent and generous documen-

Proceedings on Adjournment of Motion tary on the aspect of the industry, recreation, fish, game and wildlife existing together as a resource. In May 1961, the federation of rod and gun clubs of B.C., adopted the brief as their official document, an advisory offering to the B.C. hydro authorities as a token of good faith in a cooperative covenant they believed existed between them.
Therefore, be it resolved, in the interests of this association and all citizens of B.C. that-
A.	All dam controlled reservoirs in the Columbia system be cleaned as specified in the west Kootenay rod and gun clubs zone brief: "All vegetation must be cleared from the present low water level up to 10 feet of elevation above the maximum storage level. This is an absolute necessity, if use is to be made of the reservoir for any purposes mentioned in this brief other than storage power generation."
B.	And be it further resolved that-
All reservoir clearing as aforementioned, be completed prior to initial flooding.
Voted upon and accepted unanimously at a regular meeting of the Nelson rod and gun club, February 19, 1965.
J. J. McEwan, Committee chairman
This situation has caused a great deal of concern in Kootenay West, and this resolution has been sponsored by chambers of commerce and other organizations. It is the cause of editorials in the Nelson Daily News and other newspapers, because if we are not able to get these basins cleared according to the program laid out by the rod and gun clubs, we will have lost tremendous possibilities for the development of our natural resources.
The Nelson Daily News of March 17, 1965 said in part:
Grave fears are being expressed by area conservationists and businessmen that the government is planning to divert funds, some $68 million, slated for clearance work to other channels.
That is the government of B.C.
The reservoirs are destined to become a sportsman's and tourist's paradise... if properly established. Improper clearance can endanger all of this, as well as create huge expense for repairs to damage caused by floating debris.
The people of this province should utilize every means at their command to see that the government does not shirk its responsibilities in this regard.
I brought this question up, Mr. Speaker, because it is a matter of great concern to thousands in my constituency, and I want to find out from the minister what he considers the responsibility of the federal government with respect to these fishery resources in particular.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as we seem this evening, for the first time in quite some time, to have reverted to a two party system, I want to tell the hon. member I appreciate the interest

Proceedings on Adjournment of Motion which has been shown by the united conservation front of Kootenay West in this vital problem affecting the sport and commercial fisheries of B.C. The hon. member stated that the federal government was responsible for the conservation of commercial and sport fishing in British Columbia. I wish to assure him that 1 am fully aware of the circumstances involved in the building of the Columbia river dam. However, I must inform the hon. member that the management of fresh water fishing in British Columbia is by agreement the responsibility of the government of that province. The province has been kept fully aware of the situation and has been advised from time to time of ways and means of preventing any possible difficulties which may arise from the construction of such important projects as the one mentioned by the hon. gentleman.
Furthermore, the management of freshwater fishing in British Columbia has fully co-operated at all times with the federal Department of Fisheries and I can assure the hon. member that all possible steps are being taken to see that the fish population will not be affected as a result of this gigantic project which means so much to the population of his province.

maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-ASSISTANCE TO DISPLACED WORKERS IN AUTOMOBILE INDUSTRY
LABOUR CONDITIONS-ASSISTANCE TO DISPLACED WORKERS IN AUTOMOBILE INDUSTRY
speechtext:
The matter I wish to raise concerns the recently signed auto pact between the United States and Canada. It is related to a question which I placed before the Minister of Industry on March 24. At that time I was drawing attention to fears which have been expressed about unemployment caused by a reduction of staff in Windsor. I was unable to obtain from the minister a commitment similar to that given by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) to the effect that there would be no such dislocation.
The situation is this. The president of Chrysler has announced that the company will be producing an additional 80,000 units of their 1966 model for export to the United States. This means a reduction in what is called the model mix, and the production of a reduced number of models. This in turn means a cutback in the number of office employees needed to follow through what would otherwise be a wide variety of models. In the product engine department of the Ford Motor Company of Canada approximately 250 employees will lose their jobs due to the reallocation of their
[Mr. Robichaud.l
duties to the parent company in the United States as a result of this agreement. A few of these people have been interviewed by Ford Motor Company of the United States, but even though the supervisors said they were acceptable they have been notified by the personnel department of the U.S. company that they were unacceptable as employees.
The changes in production and the reduction in the number of models will affect the whole of the remainder of the office staff because of a reduction of the number of parts controlled in the offices. For example, in the engine plant they have 1,350 parts and subassemblies for the 1965 product. In 1966 they will have 290 parts and subassemblies for one engine instead of 11. So it is easy to see there will be a lot of empty desks. It has been calculated that 75 per cent of the workers in the engine plant of Ford will be affected. The Chrysler office staff will not be affected until the latter part of 1965 and 1966 as a result of advance tooling for the 1966 model year. But after 1966 Chrysler will follow the same general pattern of disintegration.
In 1967 both Ford and Chrysler will be dropping their car lines to three models. This will eliminate about 50 per cent of the parts handled by the office staff. It is estimated that the following production and office plan operations will be affected: production control follow up department; production control specification department; production control scheduling department; production control engineering department; production control drafting department; plant engineering department; blue print department; invoice auditing department; accounts receivable department; accounts payable department; customs department; purchasing department; sales department; technical department; pricing department; accounting department; payroll department; service parts department, and typists.
We would like to have some statement from the government in amplification of the remarks of the Minister of Industry as to what policies and programs are available to offset the real and genuine fears being expressed by the people of Windsor about the possible loss of jobs and dislocation of the industry, which may well result from the present agreement.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of Labour):
maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-ASSISTANCE TO DISPLACED WORKERS IN AUTOMOBILE INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) has now joined the hon. members for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and Essex

West (Mr. Gray) in drawing to my attention and to the attention of the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) the situation that may prevail as a result of the duty free entry of automobiles between Canada and the United States. It should be pointed out that the purpose of the agreement is to increase substantially the total volume of Canadian production, and this can be expected over the course of time to result in an increase in total job opportunities in the Canadian industry. Therefore any manpower adjustments that may be required will take place in the context of expanding employment.
We have had meetings already with the united automobile workers in Ottawa, directed at foreseeing what adjustments may take place and in an effort to establish arrangements to assist in these adjustments. I have had a meeting, also, with the president of Chrysler, at which he stated in the presence of the Secretary of State for External Affairs and myself that there would be no reduction in the number of office workers required in his operations. The same situation, I understand, prevails with respect to Ford Motor Company of Canada.
Proceedings on Adjournment of Motion
These changes that may take place will take place in a context of expanding employment, but there may be adjustments required for individual workers. Our purpose, in addition to discussing the matter with the representatives of the union, is to convene very soon a meeting with the company presidents and company heads with a view to establishing joint arrangements between management and the unions to prepare for adjustments that may affect individual workers, and to set in motion the kind of programs that will assist in the adjustment, including training and especially the use of the manpower consultative service of the Department of Labour. I am expecting that we will get the full cooperation of the union and management in working out joint arrangements that will prepare for any displacements, and reduce to a minimum any adjustment problem posed for individual workers.
